passage: The river below the old bridge in Kothapeta was brown and fast after the rains. Karthik's cousins were already climbing the rail, whooping, and dropping feet-first into the water one after another. "Asif, come on! Everyone's done it!" Asif looked down. The current pulled at a branch and swallowed it. His stomach turned over. But nobody else looked worried; they were laughing, shaking water from their hair on the bank. Maybe I'm just a coward, he thought. Karthik slapped his back. "It's nothing, yaar." Asif climbed over the rail, held his breath and jumped. The cold hit like a slap, and the current dragged him sideways for a long, frightening moment before he grabbed a root. On the bank, the others cheered. Asif didn't feel like cheering.

qa.q: What happened to the branch Asif watched in the river?
qa.a: The current pulled at it and swallowed it.

qa.q: Why did Asif doubt the fear felt on the bridge?
qa.a: Nobody else looked worried, so Asif decided the fear must mean being a coward rather than a real warning.

qa.q: Where was the turning point for Asif, and what could Asif have done there instead?
qa.a: The moment Asif's stomach turned at the current was the turning point; Asif could have trusted that feeling and stayed on the bank, saying the water looked too strong today.

qa.q: What might Karthik have missed while saying "It's nothing"?
qa.a: Caught up in the fun, Karthik probably missed Asif's fear and how strong the current was, because the group's laughter made it all look safe.

grounding: A teenager jumps into a swollen river because the group seems at ease, overriding a strong private unease.

passage: Early December in Utrecht, and the canal behind the school had frozen for the first time. By four o'clock half of Felix's year group was out on it, sliding, filming each other, shrieking. "It's solid," Aiko called from the middle. "Everyone's on it!" Felix stood on the bank in his heavy boots. The ice near the reeds looked grey, not white, and he had heard it tick. There had been only two nights of frost. Still, thirty people couldn't all be stupid, could they? Maybe he was the nervous one who always spoiled things. He stepped down. Halfway across, something cracked like a knuckle. Everyone froze, then laughed. Felix laughed too, too loudly, and walked very carefully back to the bank, heart hammering.

qa.q: How many nights of frost had there been?
qa.a: Only two nights of frost.

qa.q: What was going on in Felix's mind while standing on the bank?
qa.a: Felix noticed the grey ice and the ticking but told himself thirty people couldn't all be wrong, and worried about being the one who spoils things.

qa.q: Which moment could have gone differently for Felix, and how?
qa.a: Just before stepping down, Felix could have trusted the grey ice and the ticking sound and stayed on the bank, maybe calling the others off.

qa.q: How might Aiko see things after hearing the crack?
qa.a: Aiko, who had called the ice solid, might suddenly realise the group's confidence was just everyone copying each other, and feel shaken too. 😰

grounding: A teenager walks onto thin canal ice because the whole group seems comfortable, overriding his own doubts.

passage: At the district cricket academy, the new craze was batting against the bowling machine without a helmet. "Real batters read the ball," Akash said, cranking the speed dial up another notch. One by one the under-17 squad took their turn, bareheaded, grinning for the phone camera. Aparna unbuckled her helmet slowly. Her mother had saved for two months to buy it, and her fingers didn't want to let go. But everyone was laughing, even Rohini, who was usually careful. So maybe the fear was just her being soft. She set the helmet on the bench and took guard. The third ball reared off a crack in the mat and hissed past her ear. The nets went quiet. Aparna stayed at the crease, bat shaking, and pretended to grin.

qa.q: What was the new craze at the district cricket academy?
qa.a: Batting against the bowling machine without a helmet.

qa.q: What do Aparna's fingers holding on to the helmet suggest?
qa.a: They suggest Aparna's own judgment was saying no; the fear was real, even though the group's laughter made it seem silly.

qa.q: At what moment could Aparna have chosen differently, and what might that look like?
qa.a: While unbuckling the helmet, Aparna could have kept it on and batted anyway; one careful player makes it easier for others to do the same.

qa.q: How might Akash feel when the ball hissed past Aparna's ear?
qa.a: Akash, who kept turning up the speed, might suddenly feel scared and responsible, seeing that the challenge was dangerous rather than brave.

grounding: A teenager removes her helmet for a risky trend because the whole squad seems at ease, doubting her own fear.

passage:
Dear Gautam Bhaiya,
You asked why I sounded strange on the phone on Sunday. Here's the truth.
On Saturday night the whole group climbed the ladder on our building's water tank to take photos. Everyone went up laughing, even Shreya, who is scared of lifts. The rungs were rusty and one wobbled. My stomach kept saying no. But they all looked so relaxed, I thought maybe the problem was just me being the scaredy little sister again. So I climbed.
Halfway up my foot slipped. I scraped my palm open and hung there shaking till Neel pulled me back down.
Nobody else seemed worried at all. I keep wondering if they were just pretending too.
I told Mummy that night. She cleaned my hand, and she wasn't even angry, just quiet.
Jaya

qa.q: What happened to Jaya's foot halfway up the ladder?
qa.a: Her foot slipped, and she scraped her palm open and hung there shaking.

qa.q: What was Jaya thinking when her stomach kept saying no?
qa.a: She thought the problem might be her being the scaredy little sister, because everyone else looked so relaxed.

qa.q: At which moment could Jaya have trusted her own unease, and what might she have done?
qa.a: When she felt the wobbly rung and her stomach said no, she could have stayed on the ground and taken photos from there.

qa.q: What might Gautam Bhaiya feel on reading Jaya's letter?
qa.a: He might feel shaken that she got hurt, and glad she told Mummy and was honest with him.

grounding: A teen joins a risky climb because the group seems calm, doubting her own fear.

passage: Okay, Vinita, you want the chilli story for the show. Fine, here's Rafiq's most embarrassing night. I was sixteen, at my cousin's wedding in Hyderabad. The boys, me included, found a packet of those extreme-hot chips, the kind with the warning on the pack. One chip each, on camera. Every one of them did it, laughing, fanning their mouths, acting cool. I remember thinking: my eyes are already watering from the smell. That's a sign, right? But nobody else looked worried. So I told myself I was the problem. I ate it. Ten minutes later I was throwing up behind the tent and my Ammi was holding my head. Later my cousin Irfan admitted his stomach hurt all night too. He just didn't say. So, Vinita, that's the thing. I wasn't the only one scared. I was just the only one who thought it was only me.

qa.q: Where was Rafiq when he ate the chilli chip?
qa.a: He was at his cousin's wedding in Hyderabad.

qa.q: What did Rafiq believe about his watering eyes before he ate the chip?
qa.a: He sensed it was a warning sign but decided he was the problem, because nobody else looked worried.

qa.q: What did Rafiq learn from Irfan's admission that could change how he decides next time?
qa.a: He learned others may hide the same fear, so their calm faces aren't proof something is safe, and his own warning signs count.

qa.q: How might Irfan see the evening now, knowing Rafiq was also scared?
qa.a: Irfan might realise that by hiding his own pain he helped make the dare look easy, and feel a bit responsible.

grounding: A teen goes along with a risky food dare because the group looks comfortable, overriding his own unease.
